definitions.definition: A rule that says the strength of something (like gravity or light) gets weaker by the square of the distance from its source.
definitions.example: If you double your distance from a campfire, you get only one-quarter of the heat.

definitions.definition: A special number (about 1/137) that controls how strongly tiny particles like electrons interact with light.
definitions.example: It's like a dial that sets how bright atoms glow when they absorb or release energy.

definitions.definition: The event about 13.8 billion years ago when the universe began expanding from an extremely hot, dense state.
definitions.example: Think of it as the starting point of everything we see in the sky.

definitions.definition: The smallest possible unit of time, about 10⁻⁴³ seconds, after which our current laws of physics can describe the universe.
definitions.example: It's like the shortest tick of the universe's clock.

definitions.definition: The process where two small atomic nuclei smash together to form a larger one, releasing huge amounts of energy.
definitions.example: This is how the Sun makes its heat and light.

definitions.definition: The branch of physics that describes how very tiny things like atoms and electrons behave, often in strange ways.
definitions.example: It explains why electrons can be in two places at once, like a spinning coin that is both heads and tails until you look.

definitions.definition: Waves of electric and magnetic energy that travel through space, including light, radio waves, and X-rays.
definitions.example: Sunlight and the signals from a Wi-Fi router are both forms of electromagnetic radiation.

definitions.definition: A set of four rules that describe how electricity and magnetism work together, especially as waves.
definitions.example: They explain why a magnet can push a wire and why light can travel through empty space.

definitions.definition: Einstein's theory that says the laws of physics are the same for all observers moving at constant speed, and that the speed of light is always the same.
definitions.example: It explains why time slows down for someone moving very fast, like in a spaceship near light speed.

definitions.definition: Einstein's famous equation that says energy (E) equals mass (m) times the speed of light (c) squared, meaning a tiny amount of mass can become a huge amount of energy.
definitions.example: This is how nuclear power plants and the Sun produce energy.

definitions.definition: A fixed number that tells how strong gravity is between any two objects with mass.
definitions.example: It's like the 'strength setting' for gravity in the universe.

definitions.definition: The fastest speed anything can travel in the universe, about 300,000 kilometers per second.
definitions.example: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.

definitions.definition: Not made of physical stuff; existing without a body or matter.
definitions.example: A thought or a number is immaterial—you can't touch it or weigh it.

definitions.definition: Having no beginning and no end; existing forever.
definitions.example: The number 2 has always been true and will always be true, even if all humans disappear.

definitions.definition: Based on reason and logic; able to be understood by thinking.
definitions.example: A math proof is rational because it follows clear steps that make sense.

definitions.definition: The underlying layer or foundation that supports something else.
definitions.example: Soil is the substrate for a garden—it holds the roots and provides nutrients.

definitions.definition: The ability to cause something to happen or to have an effect.
definitions.example: A rock has causal power because it can break a window if thrown.

definitions.definition: Working or in effect; actively doing something.
definitions.example: The rules of a game are operative from the moment you start playing.

definitions.definition: To put something into a clear, written, and organized form, often using symbols or rules.
definitions.example: A scientist formalizes a discovery by writing it as an equation or a law.

definitions.definition: The part of the universe we can see from Earth, limited by how far light has traveled since the Big Bang.
definitions.example: It's like the horizon of a ship at sea—you can only see so far.

definitions.definition: A Greek word (pronounced 'LOH-gos') meaning 'word,' 'reason,' 'order,' or 'logic.' In the Bible, it refers to the rational principle that underlies the universe.
definitions.example: Think of it as the 'blueprint' or 'logic code' that makes the universe run smoothly.

definitions.definition: The scientific name for modern humans, the species we belong to.
definitions.example: You and everyone you know are Homo sapiens.

definitions.definition: Short for 'Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica,' Isaac Newton's famous book that laid out the laws of motion and gravity.
definitions.example: It's like the instruction manual for how objects move on Earth and in space.
